# Time and Tsibbles

The retail_ts data is the advance monthly sales for retail and food services from the U.S. Census Bureau, measured in millions of dollar and seasonally adjusted, and going from January 1992 to the most recent month. The can_gas data holds monthly gas production in Canada that is measured in billions of cubic meters, from January 1960 to February 2005.

Building Tsibble

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "retail_sales_raw.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)

retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), 
               names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)
has_gaps(retail_ts)
```

Canadian Gas Production

```{r}
key_vars(canadian_gas)
index_var(canadian_gas)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume)
has_gaps(can_gas)

```

Working with Dates in a Tsibble

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))

can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(year    = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))

can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume))

can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
```

Changing the Frequency of a Series

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume)
```

We sum() the monthly values because they represent the total amount produced each month;instead, a mean() would just give the "typical month" value. Yes, quarter series still shows seasonality because production differs between quarters, meaning that seasonal patterns are still observable.

U.S. retail sales data with just one line:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)
```

 Plot and compare the two lines:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The NSA series shows a repeating seasonal pattern every year, in which in December sales spike and then drop every January. The SA series follows the same pattern because the adjustment does not change the movement in sales. The SA series is in fact smoother than the NSA series, but it follows the same #behavior in the long-run.

Canadian gas production series:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas |> 
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Billions of cubic meters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales with Trend Line:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales with Trend Line",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +

```

I decided to add the geom_smooth() to highlight the trend in sales to make the the information clear and easier to observe.

# Transformations

The seasonal swings of can_gas do in fact get larger as the series grows, with spikes and drops over the years. There is an upward increase over the sample series, but it is not constant. It increases rapidly during the 1960s and early 1970s, grows slower and almost flat from the mid-1970s to the late 1980s, and then #increases rapidly again during the 1990s.

Log of Canadian Gas Production:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Canadian Gas Production",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log(Volume)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

After taking the logs, the seasonal swings became more consistent in size over time and it appears more uniform. The transformation made it smoother but it didn't completely make it series linear and it still changes over time. I think logs are a good idea for can_gas. Even though they did not make trend perfectly linear, they did improve the series by making the seasonal swings more constant. Being able to see the nonlinear behavior in growth in an easier model does in fact help.

Month-over-Month Growth Rate in Canadian Gas Production:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth Rate in Canadian Gas Production",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Percent Growth"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Growth Rate Difference Between Direct and Log-Difference:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth Rate Difference Between Direct and Log-Difference",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Absolute Difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

I think the log difference approximation is good since the absolute difference is usually small, although there are some large gaps.

Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The NSA series is noisier with large positive and negative spikes throughout the month-over-month growth rate. The SA series is much more narrow and ranges around zero. The reason the NSA series is noisy is because it still contains the seasonal patterns, similarly to what we observed in 2.7b.

# Seasonality

Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The SA series is smoother and has less variation than the NSA series, showing that is seasonally adjusted. The NSA series shows a repeating seasonal pattern, with more spikes and drops in sales.

Seasonal Pattern in Log of Canadian Gas Production:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in Log of Canadian Gas Production",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log(Volume)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The seasonal pattern shows that gas production is higher during the winter months and lower during the summer months. This matches my intuition because usually there is more demand for natural gas during the winter months since people use it for heating due to the colder weather.

Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )
```

X-13ARIMA_SEATS Decomposition:

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()
retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

The seasonal factor is highest in December and roughly at 1.2, meaning that sales are about 20% above trend during that season. The size of the seasonal swings appear to be stable over time with similar peaks and drops each year.

My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's:

```{r}
#| echo: false
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

My X-13 seasonal adjustment appears to be very similar to the Census Bureau's because the the difference is relatively small around 0%. They do differ the most around 2020 to 2023, where a gap exceeds 1%.

Estimated Everage Monthly Growth Rate of Gas Production

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))
report(can_gas_fit)

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The month with the most significant seasonal effect June with the largest t-statistic of 4.777.

Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The fitted line fits poorly in the early years of the sample, but is does well in capturing the seasonal pattern and follows that upward trend well.

Ljung-Box Test:

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24)
```

The residuals do not appear to be white noise because they show a long-run pattern and a strong autocorrelation. The Ljung-Box test rejects the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation at the 5% level.

# Forecast Evaluation

Expanding-Window TS-CV with a First Training Sample of 240 months (20 years):

```{r}
#| echo: false
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))

results_tbl <- tibble(
  Model = c("SNAIVE", "TSLM"),
  MAE = c(0.562, 4.010),
  RMSE = c(0.702, 4.360)
)

results_tbl |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The first forecast evaluated is January 1980 and the last forecast evaluated is March 2005. The SNAIVE model produces more accurate forecasts because it has a lower MAE and RMSE than the TSLM model. Both metrics agree that the SNAIVE model performs better than TSLM model.

Diebold–Mariano test with absolute loss:

```{r}
#| echo: false
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

The DM statistic is -31.278 and the p-value is \<2.2e-16. We reject the null hypothesis that the two models are equally accurate and conclude that the SNAIVE model performs better.

A Rolling Window of 240 months:

```{r}
#| echo: false
gas_cv_fc_roll <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc_roll |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) 

results_tbl2 <- tibble(
  Model = c("SNAIVE", "TSLM"),
  MAE = c(0.562, 2.090),
  RMSE = c(0.702, 2.420)
)

results_tbl2 |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The TSLM model's accuracy changed more when switching to a rolling window. The MAE and RMSE decreased for the TSLM model, while the SNAIVE model's accuracy stayed basically the same. This makes sense because the fitted line trend from part 4.4b did not fit the entire sample well.

# Reflection

The residual check in Part 4.4c did not look like they had noise, which was kind of weird because the part stated that a well-specified model should leave residuals that look like white noise. I think I would have liked to see how a model with white noise looks like, in order to be able to compare models with and without white noise. The forecast evaluation was really clear in what it was searching for and what the results of the evaluation mean. The SNAIVE model ended up being the one with the best performance, but I would have liked to see a situation in which that was not true throughout Part 5.
